title: A First-Timer's Nature & Outdoor Tour from Seoul: 2 Nights, 3 Days Itinerary
html:
Most "first-timer" Korea itineraries are built around palaces, shopping streets, and K-pop landmarks. This one is different: it's for travelers who want to see mountains, gardens, and river views in between the city sightseeing. You don't need any hiking experience or your own car for this trip — everything below is reachable by subway, train, or an easy-to-book bus.

This is a 2-night, 3-day plan: one day inside Seoul, one full day trip to Gapyeong (a county about 1–1.5 hours northeast of Seoul, home to several of Korea's best-known nature spots), and a slow final morning back in the city before you head to your next stop or the airport.

Day 1: A Morning Hike Up Bukhansan, Then Sunset by the Han River


Bukhansan National Park. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Bukhansan (literally "mountain north of the Han River") is a national park right on the edge of Seoul, and it's the easiest real mountain hike you can do without leaving the city. There are two routes beginners should know about:

  • Easier route (Gireum side): Take subway Line 4 to Gireum Station, Exit 3, then bus 110B or 143 to the last stop (about 13 minutes). From there it's a gentle 10-minute walk to the park entrance, followed by wide, well-maintained trails.
  • Classic route (Bukhansanseong Fortress Course): Take subway Line 3 to Gupabal Station, Exit 1, then bus 34, 704, or 8772 to the "Bukhansanseong" stop (about 17 minutes). This is the most popular trail — mostly gentle, with one steeper, rocky section near the top if you push on toward Baegundae Peak. A relaxed round trip on the lower part of this course takes about 2–3 hours; most first-timers don't need to summit to enjoy it.

The park is free to enter, open roughly from 4:00 to 17:00 in warmer months (shorter hours in winter), and hiking after dark isn't allowed. Wear real walking shoes — sandals and smooth-soled sneakers get slippery on the granite rock. Bring water; there isn't much to buy once you're past the entrance.

💡 How locals actually do it: Korean hikers almost always finish with a meal near the trailhead — usually pajeon (a savory pancake) and a bowl of makgeolli (a mildly sweet, slightly fizzy rice wine) at one of the small restaurants by the entrance. You don't have to drink, but trying the pancake is worth it.


Yeouido Hangang Park, one of the most popular riverside parks for picnics and sunset views. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

After you've showered and rested, head to the Han River (Hangang) for the evening. Yeouido Hangang Park (subway Line 5, Yeouinaru Station, Exit 2 or 3) is one of the easiest riverside parks to reach and a favorite spot for watching the sunset over the water.

💡 How locals actually do it: Instead of packing a picnic from home, most Koreans buy cheap mats, snacks, and the famous ramyeon (instant noodles) at the convenience store right inside the park, then cook the noodles at the store's own hot-water machine and eat outside by the river. Some people even order chicken delivery straight to a riverside bench — delivery apps in Seoul really do deliver to parks, not just addresses. It's one of the most "Seoul" things you can do on a clear evening.

Day 2: Nami Island and the Garden of Morning Calm (Gapyeong Day Trip)


The tree-lined paths on Nami Island, Gapyeong. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Nami Island (Namiseom) is a small, half-moon-shaped island on a river near Gapyeong, famous for its long rows of metasequoia and ginkgo trees. It became internationally known through the K-drama Winter Sonata, and it's playful about its fame — the island calls itself the "Naminara Republic," a fictional micro-country, and will even stamp a mock "passport" at the entrance.

To get there from Seoul, take the ITX-Cheongchun train (an intercity express, a step up from the regular subway) from Yongsan or Cheongnyangni Station to Gapyeong Station, then a short local bus or taxi to the ferry pier. The short ferry ride (included in most ticket prices) is the only way onto the island — there's no bridge for regular visitors. As of this writing, adult admission (with the return ferry included) runs around ₩16,000, but island ticket prices do change, so check the official Nami Island website before your trip.

Here's how the main transport options from Seoul compare:

OptionApprox. cost (one-way)Approx. timeBest for
ITX-Cheongchun train₩5,700–6,90040–55 min to Gapyeong Stn.Most travelers — fast, comfortable, easy to book
Regular subway (Gyeongchun Line)~₩2,50090–120 minBudget travelers with no rush
Direct shuttle bus₩18,000–28,000 (round trip)~70–90 minTravelers who want door-to-door pickup in central Seoul


One of the themed gardens at the Garden of Morning Calm, Gapyeong. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

In the afternoon, head to the Garden of Morning Calm (Achim Goyo Sumogwon), a large botanical garden with more than twenty themed sections and over 5,000 plant species. From Gapyeong Station, a local bus or roughly 20-minute taxi ride gets you there; there's also a hop-on, hop-off Gapyeong City Tour Bus day pass for travelers visiting multiple spots in the area. Adult admission is around ₩11,000 — again, confirm the current price before you go, since garden ticket prices are updated from time to time. If you're visiting in late autumn or winter, ask locally about seasonal light displays — the garden runs a well-known lighting festival for part of the year.

Since this is a 2-night trip, plan to stay overnight in the Gapyeong area rather than rushing back to Seoul the same day. You don't need a car to do this: many riverside guesthouses and glamping sites near Gapyeong Station or the Nami Island ferry pier are a short taxi ride away, and quite a few will arrange pickup from the station if you message the host in advance through the booking app. Book a few weeks ahead if you're traveling on a spring or autumn weekend, since this area fills up fast with domestic tourists too.

Day 3: Seoul Forest and a Slow Bike Ride Along the Han River


Seoul Forest, a large park built on the site of a former water treatment facility. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Take the train back to Seoul in the morning, then ease into your last day at Seoul Forest (subway Line 2, Seoul Forest Station). It's a large, free park split into a few different zones — a cultural area, an eco-forest, a wetland garden, and a stretch that runs right along the Han River, plus a small deer enclosure that's popular with families.

This is also the easiest place in Seoul to try Ttareungi, Seoul's public bike-share system (sometimes written "Seoul Bike"). You don't need to make an account in advance — you can rent through the app on the spot with a foreign credit card. Rates are roughly ₩1,000 per hour, and docking stations are all over the park and along the riverside bike path. Ride along the Han River path toward Ttukseom for about 20–30 easy minutes, then dock the bike and walk the rest.

💡 How locals actually do it: Seoulites rarely plan a dedicated "bike trip" — they just grab a Ttareungi bike for one short leg of a longer day, the same way you'd hop on a bus. Don't feel like you need to ride for hours; even a 20-minute stretch along the river is how most people actually use it.

Wrap up with lunch near Seoul Forest or Seongsu-dong (the trendy café neighborhood right next to the park) before heading to your next destination.

🌲 Thinking about adding a hike or a river afternoon to your own Korea trip? Drop your questions in the comments below — happy to help you plan it out!
meta_description: A beginner-friendly 2-night, 3-day Korea itinerary for nature lovers: Bukhansan hike, Nami Island, Garden of Morning Calm, Han River.
